overview: Hypacrosaurus altispinus was a large lambeosaurine hadrosaur from the late Campanian and early Maastrichtian of Alberta and Montana (~75–67 Ma), bearing a tall hollow crest similar to Corythosaurus. Remarkable nest sites from the Two Medicine Formation preserve eggs, embryos, hatchlings and juveniles at different growth stages — providing detailed data on hadrosaur developmental biology.

Bone histology from Hypacrosaurus growth series shows that it grew from a 50-cm hatchling to a 9-metre adult in as little as 10–12 years — among the fastest growth rates documented for any dinosaur — before slowing sharply at maturity. Proteins extracted from Hypacrosaurus eggshell fragments have been proposed as among the oldest biological molecules preserved in fossils, though this remains debated.

articles.title: Nesting and early development
articles.body: Nesting sites in the Two Medicine Formation preserve complete clutches of Hypacrosaurus eggs (spherical, about 20 cm diameter) and hatchlings with incompletely formed skulls and limb bones. The developmental sequence documents how the hollow crest formed progressively through ontogeny — small in juveniles, full-sized in adults — paralleling the pattern in Corythosaurus.

articles.title: Growth rates
articles.body: Bone histology shows one of the fastest known growth rates among hadrosaurs: reaching adult size in 10–12 years. The growth rings (lines of arrested growth) record annual growth cycles, showing rapid juvenile growth that decelerated sharply at maturity. This pattern mirrors fast-growing large mammals and is inconsistent with ectothermic (cold-blooded) physiology.

articles.title: Ancient proteins controversy
articles.body: A 2020 paper reported osteopontin (a bone matrix protein) extracted from 75-million-year-old Hypacrosaurus eggshell — potentially the oldest biological molecule identified from a fossil. The interpretation is controversial: contamination by microbial biofilms or other modern sources cannot be fully excluded at this age, and independent verification has not yet confirmed the result.

record.mya: early Maastrichtian, roughly 71-69 million years ago for H. altispinus
record.description: Hypacrosaurus altispinus was a tall-spined lambeosaurine hadrosaurid from the Horseshoe Canyon Formation of Alberta. Several skulls and skeletons document a hollow-crested herbivore; famous nests, eggs and embryos belong to the distinct species H. stebingeri and must not be attributed automatically to H. altispinus.
facts: The tall neural spines formed a deep back profile, not necessarily a thin sail.
The hollow crest contained nasal passages plausibly involved in sound production, though exact calls are modelled.
Nesting and embryology evidence is species-specific to H. stebingeri.

review.ageReviewNote: Corrected to early Maastrichtian for H. altispinus; the profile must not use the older Two Medicine age of H. stebingeri.

Crest acoustics and display are biomechanical inferences.
